Then it becomes a "red letter day" for the accused? :)

This comment actually started out as a joke, but then it occurred to me that could very well be what happens….a "sure conviction" becomes a "surprise acquittal" with the effects mentioned at the end ("Nonetheless, successfully employed, SCP-141 is an almost surefire conviction. Even in the event of exoneration, "guilty" subjects will often still be ostracized and viewed as guilty by influenced witnesses and law enforcement personnel, who may in some cases [DATA REDACTED].") being flipped…..even if everyone else in the world KNOWS the person is guilty, those influenced are completely convinced of their innocence.

Who knows…the book could be the basis for the phrase. ;)

item.content:encoded:
I seem to recall codices had been invented as early as the first century CE, derived from the writing tablets used regularly in Roman times. The Republic ended around the 27 BCE, so perhaps I should change it to early Imperial latin. Not sure how distinct the differences would be.

As for the second, feel free to edit it for correctness. While I've got a BA in history, the Roman era isn't my specialty. I do know, however, that the word damnatio was in use to refer to the concept of damnatio memoriae- the daming or destruction of all records of an individual, sometimes applied in treason cases. The idea I had was that this was originally devised for use in the proscription trials.

Hey, I'm not a regular contributor or anything but I felt I must comment because I really like this SCP and I am currently in graduate school studying Classics. I don't have anything really to add as far as the story or actual item is concerned because I think it is really good as is, but as you seem writing with an eye for history I thought I would be the ass hole who chimes in on that stuff.
1. The Romans had no bound books until very late antiquity. Everything was written on scrolls.
2. If you are insisting that the book only understands "Republican Latin," then it would not understand its own title which to Cicero would literally mean "treebark the loss at court." (codex meaning book only in late antique and medieval periods)
suggestions: liber damnationum or liber damnatorum (the book of losses at court / the book of those found guilty)

item.content:encoded:
I do think it is a cool idea, indeed. Unfortunately, I want one, because I am an evil person… and I have studied Latin, the Roman Republic, and associated areas.

As a suggestion? Force it to all be in Latin, and squeeze modern concepts into something that you could explain to a citizen of the Roman Republic. That raises the bar of difficulty to just use it a bit higher, I think, and goes better with the theme. Not only that, but it would help people who were skilled practitioners, since you wouldn't need to work out how to explain a personal computer over and over again.

That would tend to give a sense of power to the habitual user as well. Nothing by the artifact itself, just by the old adage of Power Corrupts. Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?
